methodological_rigor.justification: Comprehensive in vivo tumor modeling study using mtDNA-deficient (ρ0) cancer cells in mice, evaluating horizontal mitochondrial transfer (HMT) as therapeutic vulnerability. Multiple cell line backgrounds tested. Proper genetic controls (ρ0, ρ0+AOX, DHODH-deleted variants). Measurement of mitochondrial transfer frequency and tumor growth kinetics. Assessment of tumor microenvironment composition (immune and stromal cells) by flow cytometry/immunohistochemistry. Statistical testing with P-values reported. In vivo experiments with appropriate group sizes.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Preclinical mechanistic study identifying de novo pyrimidine synthesis via DHODH as essential for tumor progression in mtDNA-deficient cancers. Shows cancer cells exploit mitochondrial transfer from stromal cells (MSCs) to restore respiration and DHODH function. Suggests therapeutic vulnerability through DHODH inhibition. Relevant to understanding metabolic plasticity and tumor microenvironment cooperation, but clinical applicability limited without identifying mtDNA-deficient tumors in patients.

reporting_quality.justification: Methods section adequately describes mouse xenograft protocols, DHODH genetic deletion approach, and mitochondrial transfer detection methods. Ethics approvals referenced. However, quantification of mitochondrial transfer frequency in tumors could be more explicit, specifics on flow cytometry gating strategy not provided, and analytical methods for MSC identification/recruitment not fully detailed. No explicit data availability statement or code sharing.

novelty_literature.justification: Demonstrates functional importance of horizontal mitochondrial transfer in tumor progression through DHODH-dependent pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Concept of HMT in cancer previously established; contribution is identifying specific functional consequence (pyrimidine synthesis) and showing DHODH inhibition blocks tumor growth. Identifies stromal cell involvement (MSCs as mitochondrial donors) which is somewhat novel. Mechanistic insight meaningful but incremental.

writing_presentation.justification: Clear introduction establishing mitochondrial dysfunction in cancer and recent discovery of HMT. Methods adequately described for main experimental approaches. Results section logically presents ρ0 cell biology, AOX experiments, DHODH requirement, and HMT-dependent tumor growth. Figures support findings but could benefit from clearer labeling. Discussion appropriately contextualizes metabolic plasticity and tumor microenvironment cooperation.

key_strengths: Demonstrates functional importance of horizontal mitochondrial transfer: ρ0 cancer cells acquire mtDNA from stromal cells to restore respiration and tumor growth
Identifies de novo pyrimidine synthesis via DHODH as metabolic requirement dependent on restored oxidative phosphorylation
Shows DHODH inhibition blocks or delays ρ0 tumor growth, identifying therapeutic vulnerability linked to mitochondrial dysfunction
Implicates tumor microenvironment cells (MSCs) as mitochondrial donors, demonstrating cooperation between tumor and stromal compartments
key_concerns: Unclear clinical relevance: frequency of mtDNA-deficient or severely mtDNA-damaged cancers in human patients not established; applicability limited to rare tumor subset
Therapeutic approach unclear: DHODH inhibitors alone may not be sufficient given redundancy in pyrimidine synthesis pathways
MSC identification and recruitment mechanisms incompletely characterized; specific signals driving HMT not identified
Limited to murine xenograft models; human tumor organoid or primary patient-derived xenograft models would strengthen findings
chief_reviewer.rationale: Tier 3 paper: competent preclinical work identifying DHODH as therapeutic target in mtDNA-deficient tumors. Requires clarification of clinical applicability and identification of biomarkers predicting HMT dependency. Appropriate for specialized cancer metabolism journals; broader clinical impact limited to specific tumor subset.
